content.banner: ⚽ Football = a hard session. If a match falls on a Tue or Sat: don't also do a hard run that day — move the quality run to the next easy day, or let football BE that week's hard session and keep the runs easy. Never stack quality run + football + long run on 3 straight days; keep the day after a match easy. Max ~2 hard efforts/week (football counts) + the long run.

rows: Bulk of running — keep it TRULY easy
Race pace — MP blocks & long-run finishes
paces.note: Sessions say '@ MP' and '@ T' on purpose — run them at your goal pace: 4:00 = 5:41/km. Every pace in this table is currently an ESTIMATE — the wk-10 5K never happened, so nothing here is anchored to a real effort. The wk-16 parkrun (Sat 7 Nov) sets them properly; treat these as provisional until then.

checkpoints.intro: Plan rebuilt 14 Oct (wk 13) off actual training, not the original ramp — weeks 7–12 averaged 13.7 km. The 4:00 target is HELD, which is the ambitious read of the data: it needs the 80 km peak, and that needs weeks like 7–12 to not happen again. Wk 16 re-anchors your paces; the Wk-27 half sets the final race goal (4:00 needs ~1:55).
rows: Sevilla Half — controlled, NOT a test
notes: WHY THIS CHANGED: weeks 7–12 averaged 13.7 km/week and the longest run in seven weeks was 15.7 km. Worse, that 11 Oct run was 7:36/km at 159 bpm against 21.1 km at 6:24/km and 148 bpm on 30 Aug — slower and higher-HR over a shorter distance, which is detraining, not a bad day. The original wk-13 ask (74 km, 30 km long run) was 5.4x the recent weekly average and 1.9x the longest recent run. Weeks 1–12 are left untouched as the record; 13 onward is rebuilt.

The rebuild restarts at 40 km — your own number — with a 16 km long run, ramps no more than 10% off the last comparable week, and cuts back every fourth week. Peak 80 km at wk 29 / 32 km long run. Final long run is Sun 14 Feb, three weeks out.
3:30 is kept in the table for reference only — it is not a live target after a 12-week start that produced ~165 km of running. Chasing it is how weeks 9–12 happened.
Football & other sport count as training load — see the banner above. Don't double up hard efforts or stack three hard days.

Max 2 hard run-efforts per week: Tue quality plus EITHER the Thu MP tempo OR a Sunday MP long run — never both. Hard long-run weekends always alternate with easy ones (and football still counts on top).
Rest days are Monday (always), plus Saturday through week 8 and again in the wk 13–15 rebuild; race-week Friday rest is the one exception.

The 80 km peak is load-bearing, not optional — but be clear what it is for. Sub-4 is 5:41/km and is regularly run off 50–60 km weeks; it is a pace problem more than a volume problem. The 80 km is there to make 4:00 comfortable rather than possible. So if it starts costing you weeks, drop to ~60 km and keep the consistency: 16 straight weeks at 60 beats 8 at 80 and 8 at zero, and the second pattern is what weeks 7–12 already were. Make that call at the Wk-27 half, deliberately, not by quietly missing Sundays.

Sevilla Half (Sun 6 Dec, Wk 20) — signed up alongside Cav. It arrives only 7 weeks into the rebuild, so it is a controlled long run at long-run pace, NOT a goal test. Running it hard will produce a number that scares you for no reason. The real test is the Wk-27 half on 24 Jan.

fuel.intro: You can't out-train poor fuelling, sleep or recovery — it matters a great deal more on the climb to 80 km weeks + football. Fuel the work, protect recovery, be smart about alcohol, and know when NOT to run. Fuelling a long run is a trained skill, not a race-day decision: the gut adapts over months, so practise it from the first long run rather than discovering your limits at 30 km.

sections.title: Daily diet · fuel the work
rows: Your main running fuel — don't fear it. More around long/quality days.
~1.6–2.0 g/kg/day across meals — repairs muscle & tendon as you build.
As mileage rises, under-eating causes injury, illness and burnout. Eat enough.
Veg, fruit, whole grains, quality protein, healthy fats. Check iron if chronically flat.

sections.title: Before running · what & when
rows: Fine fasted or light — coffee + banana.
Fuel first: a carb meal 2–3 h before (porridge + banana, toast + eggs), low fat/fibre.
Quick top-up if needed: banana, toast + jam, or a gel.
Caffeine is a legit, legal boost before hard sessions and races.

sections.title: During the run · carbs
rows: 30–40 g carbs/hr — one feed around 45 min, one around 90.
70–90 g/hr, every 20 min. Needs glucose AND fructose together — glucose alone saturates its transporter near 60 g/hr, however much you swallow.
Not when you feel empty. Absorption is rate-limited, so once you're behind you cannot catch up — you can only slow down.
Tolerance takes months, and it's pace-specific: carbs you handle fine at easy pace can come straight back up at MP. Build from 30–40 g/hr now toward 70–90 by the peak block.
At least two long runs with MP segments AND full race fuelling. A gel at easy pace proves nothing about a gel at marathon pace.
Per-hour rates don't change, but a 4:00 marathon is four hours of fuelling against three. Total need scales with time on feet, not distance.

sections.title: During the run · fluid & sodium
rows: 22 km on 11 Oct 2026 at ~25°C in sun: 71.1 kg -> 68.7 kg having drunk 1.0 L = 3.4 L sweat in 1.77 h. That is a HIGH rate. Plan every hot long run off it: 30 km ~4.8 L, 35 km ~5.8 L. Tokyo at 8-12°C will be roughly half.
The 1.9 L/hr figure is a hot-weather number. Weigh in before and after an evening run under 18°C to get the other end of the range — sweat loss (L) = kg lost + litres drunk.

At 1.9 L/hr a 500 ml handheld is 16 minutes of fluid. Past 90 min in heat you need a 1.5-2 L vest or a route that loops past a stash. Target 800-1000 ml/hr: you will not match the loss, but ~50% replacement keeps you inside the 2% line.
800–1,000 ml/hr — and accept you'll still finish down. At a 1.9 L/hr sweat rate even this is only half-replacement.
Lose more than 2% of body weight in fluid and both performance and heat regulation fall away sharply.
Large volumes of plain water in heat dilute blood sodium. That is genuinely dangerous, not merely suboptimal.
In heat. White crust on your cap or sunglasses and stinging eyes mean you're a salty sweater — work at the top of that range.
A run finishing above ~25°C measures heat tolerance, not fitness: HR sits 10–15 bpm higher for the same effort. Judge sessions, and time trials, on the cool ones.

sections.title: Doing it cheaply · sugar beats gels
rows: Sucrose IS glucose + fructose, bonded 1:1 — essentially the ratio brands charge a premium for, and it performs the same in head-to-head studies.

1 tbsp sugar (~12 g) + ¼ tsp table salt (~590 mg sodium) + squash to make it drinkable. That is ~2.5%, deliberately weak. 2 tbsp plus a Powerade alongside caused nausea on 7 Oct 2026; halving it to one source at 2.5% was settled fine on 11 Oct. Build the concentration back up slowly from there, one change at a time.
Stronger than that in heat and it sits in your stomach instead of emptying into the gut.
About €0.03 per 25 g of carbohydrate, against €1.80–4.00 for a gel. A €1 bag of sugar covers most of a training block.
Dates (~75 g carb/100 g — best value real food), jelly babies or Haribo, fig rolls, raisins, white bread and jam.
Late in long runs. Sugar plus caffeine, and it goes down when nothing else will.
Pennies against caffeinated gels. ~3 mg/kg an hour before a hard session or race.
Oral rehydration sachets from any pharmacy (in Spain, ask for 'suero oral') — same ingredients as tablets at a fraction of the price.
Still buy one or two gels
Try them once, so you know whether you can stomach what's on the course table when that's all there is.

Loop the route past home or the car and stash a bottle — a 7 km loop run three times needs no kit at all. A 500 ml soft flask (~€10) is the only thing worth buying before you're running 30 km in heat.

sections.title: After · recover & rehydrate
rows: After long/quality runs: carbs + 20–30 g protein within ~60 min.
Replace ~1.25–1.5× fluid lost; add salt if you're a salty/heavy sweater.

sections.title: Alcohol · the honest version
rows: Wrecks deep sleep, dehydrates, blunts recovery, raises next-day injury risk.
If you drink, do it after a hard session / before a rest day — never before a long run, quality day or race.
Minimise in the last 2 weeks; zero in race week.

sections.title: Should I run today? · quick guide
rows: Skip quality & long runs (dehydration + poor coordination = injury). Full rest or an easy jog only if mild and rehydrated first. Reschedule the key session; don't cram it back.
Pain that changes your stride or worsens as you run → STOP. 2–3 easy/off days now beats weeks off later. Sharp/one-sided/joint pain → rest & assess. Cross-train pain-free to keep fitness.
Not better in a few days, or worse? See a physio early — don't 'test it' with a hard run.
Above the neck (runny nose, mild throat) → easy run usually OK. Below the neck (chest, fever, aches) → REST. NEVER run with a fever.
Heavy legs, rising resting HR, poor sleep = under-recovery. Take the easy day easy or swap to rest. Missing one session to absorb training is smart.
If a match or tournament ate your legs, downgrade the next run to easy/recovery and protect the long run. Two hard efforts a week total — matches included.

research.intro: This plan isn't arbitrary — the phase structure, cut-back placement, hard/easy alternation and rest-day rules below are each grounded in specific training-science sources, reviewed 2026-07.

sections.title: Phase structure (5 mesocycles)
sections.detail: Base/Aerobic → Threshold intro → Lactate-Threshold + MP intro → Marathon-Specific (peak) → Taper. This matches the consensus shape across Jack Daniels (Running Formula phases I–IV), Pete Pfitzinger (Advanced Marathoning: Base / LT / Race-Prep / Taper), and Renato Canova's funnel model (General → Fundamental → Special → Specific → short taper) — all converge on 4–5 phases for a build this long, with taper length staying fixed at 2–3 weeks regardless of total plan length.

sections.title: Cut-back (deload) weeks
sections.detail: Placed every ~3–6 weeks, cutting volume ~15–25%. Sourced from Pfitzinger's step-back weeks and the broader coaching consensus (Laura Norris, RunnersConnect) of 15–33% volume drops every 3–4 weeks to let fitness consolidate before the next load increase.

sections.title: Hard/easy long-run alternation (added 2026-07-16)
sections.detail: Marathon-pace long runs now strictly alternate with easy long runs — no two hard long-run weekends back-to-back, and the weekends either side of each tune-up half are forced easy. Basis: single-run distance/intensity spikes are a stronger injury predictor than weekly-volume jumps (JOSPT running-injury literature), and "shock microcycles" (stacking hard efforts) are explicitly not recommended for sub-elite runners — steady progressive/undulating loading with regular relief outperforms them for this population.

sections.title: Max 2 hard days per week
sections.detail: Quality sessions are capped at two per week (e.g. Tue quality + EITHER Thu quality OR a hard Sunday MP long run, never all three) — consistent with polarized/pyramidal training research (Stephen Seiler) showing the bulk of volume should stay easy even as the marathon-specific phase shifts intensity distribution from ~80/20 toward ~70/30 threshold-and-MP-heavy work.

sections.title: Rest days fixed to Monday + Saturday
sections.detail: Runner preference, applied without compromising the two hard-day cap or long-run alternation above.

sections.title: Marathon-pace (MP) progression timing
sections.detail: MP segments enter the long run roughly 6–8 weeks before the peak-volume block, starting short and building toward the largest MP-block long runs at peak — the standard Pfitzinger/Hansons/Luke Humphrey pattern for when MP-specific work pays off without excess injury risk.

sections.title: Taper
sections.detail: 3-week taper, volume cut cumulatively (~roughly 75% → 50% → 30–35% of peak by race week), intensity maintained and session frequency cut ≤20% — the most robust finding in the taper literature (Mujika & Padilla's taper meta-analyses).

sections.title: Altitude training — considered, not included
sections.detail: Discussed 2026-07-16: a single week at altitude gives none of the hematological benefit (EPO/red-cell-mass adaptations need a minimum ~3–4 weeks per Levine & Stray-Gundersen's "live high, train low" research) and mostly adds hypoxic stress, poor sleep and slower paces at the wrong moment. Verdict: skip a 1-week trip; a proper 3+ week camp placed in the aerobic-base phase would be worth a separate conversation if it becomes an option.

tips: Consistency beats any single week

Weeks 7–12 averaged 13.7 km and cost you real fitness — the 11 Oct long run was slower at a higher heart rate than the one six weeks earlier. Four steady 40 km weeks are worth far more than one 80 km week followed by nothing.
Volume is the big lever

Weekly mileage moves your marathon time more than anything — that's why the rebuilt peak is 80 km. But it only counts if you stay healthy and consistent, and it has to be arrived at, not jumped to — 30 km now, 80 km in sixteen weeks, with every fourth week cut back.
Easy means easy
Your recent short runs have crept to 5:17–5:54/km while the long runs got slower. That's backwards. The base portions are 6:15–7:00/km; run them there and the long runs come good.
Football is a hard session
Treat every match as one of your two weekly hard efforts. No hard run the same day; keep the day after a match easy.
Shuffle, don't skip

Match Tuesday? Move the quality run to Wednesday and slide the easy days along. Match Saturday? Keep Sunday's long run easy, or push it to Monday if legs are cooked. Protect the long run; don't stack three hard days.
Easy means EASY
Most running should be conversational — even slower than feels 'proper'. That's where the engine is built.
The niggle rule
Pain that changes your gait or worsens = stop. 2–3 easy/off days early beats 3 weeks off later.
Guard the long run
The single most important marathon session — the last thing to sacrifice when the week gets messy.
Sleep is the #1 recovery tool
7–9 h/night. Higher volume needs more recovery, not less.
Fuel the long ones
Past 75 min take carbs on board and rehearse your race-day breakfast. Rates scale with duration — see Fuel & life for the full table.
Rotate 2 pairs of shoes
Cuts injury risk, extends shoe life (~500–800 km). Buy race shoes by the tune-up and run 3–4 sessions in them.
Warm up the hard day
10–15 min easy + a few strides before any tempo/threshold/VO2 work.
Respect cut-back weeks
The down weeks are when fitness consolidates — don't 'top them up'.
Calibrate at the half
The tune-up half sets your real race pace. Race the pace you EARNED, not the dream.
Start the race easy
First few km should feel too easy. Hold back — the marathon starts at 30 km. Even pacing wins.
Race-day fuel clock
Feed every 20–30 min from ~45 min in, with water — target 70–90 g carbs/hr over a marathon. Don't wait until you're empty.
Tokyo in early March
~8–12°C, flat, fast — a great course. Dress for ~+10°C warmer than standing; throwaway layer at the start.
Nothing new two weeks out
No new shoes, foods or bonus sessions. Lock the routine and trust the work.
Log everything
Fill it in after each run — it keeps you honest and shows patterns before they become problems.
